Rainbow palettes introduce false gradients and category boundaries, overemphasize yellows

Many RNA-seq/microarray figures map high expression to red and low to green, which is unreadable for a substantial fraction of readers with red–green CVD; the scheme also has non-uniform lightness. Nature Methods explicitly advises avoiding red–green
In the left figure we use a rainbow colour scale, which is common but can be misleading. An issue is that people sometimes perceive the brightest colour as a peak (the highest value).
Diverging palette used for strictly positive data (implied false midpoint):
Using a diverging map (e.g., blue-white-red) when the variable has no meaningful zero (all values ≥0) implies a mid reference that does not exist; use a sequential map instead.
Inconsistent color ranges across panels (destroyed comparability):
When panels auto-scale independently, identical values look different across panels;
Heatmaps of discrete matrices should usually show crisp cells; bilinear/cubic interpolation blurs structure and suggests nonexistent transitions
Aspect-ratio distortion (non-square cells). Stretching the matrix (e.g., to fit a layout) distorts block structure and spatial relationships;
Row-wise Z-scoring used without stating the interpretive trade-off.
Per-row Z-score emphasizes patterns but discards absolute magnitudes; comparisons between genes become invalid.
A single extreme drives the colormap, flattening the rest; robust limits or clipping should be considered. Practitioner threads highlight the issue and fixes.
